alt: A stepped pyramid from isolated dwelling at the base through hamlet, village, town, city and conurbation to megacity at the top. Going up, there are fewer settlements, further apart, with more high-order services and larger spheres of influence. Threshold, range and sphere of influence are defined below with examples.
caption: Bigger places need bigger thresholds, draw people from further and serve wider areas.

alt: Paired bars for fictional Norland’s five largest cities: actual sizes 3.6, 1.2, 1.0, 0.6 and 0.5 million against rank-size predictions of 3.6, 1.8, 1.2, 0.9 and 0.72 million. Every lower-ranked city falls short, and the primacy index is 3.0 against 2.0 expected.
caption: When the largest city dwarfs the rest, the country has a primate city.

alt: Two strips from city centre to edge. Burgess, based on Chicago in 1925: CBD, zone in transition, working-class homes, residential zone, commuter zone. Griffin and Ford, Latin American cities in 1980: CBD and commercial spine with an elite sector, housing declining in quality outwards, and peripheral squatter settlements at the edge.
caption: Burgess puts the better-off at the edge; Griffin and Ford put the poorest there.

alt: A bar chart of the share of plots in commercial use along one road: 85% at the centre, 55% at 0.5 km, 30% at 1 km, 15% at 2 km and 5% at 3 km. The steady fall supports the Burgess idea of a CBD with falling bid rent, but one transect cannot test Hoyt’s sectors.
caption: A steady fall with distance supports Burgess; testing sectors needs several directions.

alt: Stacked bars for fictional Norland: in 2000, 4.2 million urban and 7.8 million rural (35.0% urban); in 2020, 9.1 million urban and 6.5 million rural (58.3% urban). Urbanisation rose 23.3 percentage points while the urban population grew 116.7%.
caption: Urbanisation measures the share living in towns; urban growth measures the number.

alt: Four responses: clearance and relocation, often far from work; site-and-service plots where families build; self-help schemes such as the Orangi Pilot Project in Karachi; and upgrading in place such as Rio’s Favela-Bairro programme. Informal settlements also have workshops, markets and community networks, as in Dharavi, Mumbai.
caption: Responses range from moving people out to improving homes where they stand.

alt: Three overlapping circles, environment, economy and social fairness, meet in a central balance. Features to look for include public transport, cycling and walking routes, green space, recycling, efficient buildings, affordable housing and brownfield building. Curitiba’s bus rapid transit, flood-land parks and waste-for-food scheme are a common case study.
caption: A sustainable city balances environment, economy and fairness, now and for later residents.
